Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette: Emil had always been a private person, but after the physical abuse he suffered at the hands of his caregiver during childhood, he became increasingly withdrawn. The memories of those events still lingered, and certain triggers would send him spiraling back to that vulnerable state. A specific temperature on his skin, for instance, would transport him to the cold, damp cellar where he was often locked away. His heart racing or pounding would also bring back the panic he felt during those episodes of abuse. But it was the sudden, intrusive memories of the event that left him reeling - images of his caregiver's face, twisted in anger, would flash before his eyes without warning. As these triggers intensified, Emil began to feel a growing sense of threat. He started noticing potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment - a hammer on the workbench, a sharp edge on the kitchen counter. His body would react before he even had time to think, leaving him with a constant feeling of being "on edge." Even an unexpected touch from his wife, Maria, could startle him, making him flinch away in alarm. Emil couldn't shake the feeling that he was constantly walking on eggshells, waiting for the next blow. He became convinced that people couldn't be trusted - not even those closest to him. "You never know what can happen next," he would tell himself, a mantra of constant vigilance that left him exhausted. This sense of being an outsider, looking in at a world that seemed hostile and unforgiving, only added to his anxiety. As Emil struggled to cope with these feelings, he began to develop maladaptive strategies to avoid the triggers and threats that seemed omnipresent. He stopped paying attention to or looking at his own body, fearing what memories it might stir up. Social contacts became increasingly difficult - seeing people he had socialized with before the event only served as a painful reminder of what he had lost. And physical contact? That was out of the question altogether. But these strategies only seemed to reinforce Emil's negative appraisals. He felt like an outsider, stuck on the periphery of life, unable to connect with others or even himself. The more he avoided his own body and social contacts, the more convinced he became that people couldn't be trusted - that they were all just waiting for him to let his guard down so they could pounce. As this cycle intensified, Emil found himself back in the grip of those triggers that had started it all - memories of the event, a racing heart, a sudden chill on his skin. The threat he felt was palpable, and his body reacted before he even had time to think. It was as if he was trapped in a never-ending loop, with no escape from the pain and fear that haunted him. It was this desperation that finally brought Emil to seek help - the realization that he couldn't keep living like this, constantly on edge, waiting for the next blow. As he sat in his therapist's office, he looked around nervously, noticing the potential dangers lurking in every corner. But he knew he had to try to break free from this cycle of fear and mistrust. He was tired of being an outsider, looking in at a world that seemed hostile and unforgiving. It was time for Emil to take back control, to learn to trust himself - and maybe, just maybe, others - once again.
